faqs.question: Is a rose emoji too much if we have only just started talking?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, because 🌹 is the one flower emoji almost everyone reads as an explicit romantic statement, which removes your deniability. 🌷 or 🌸 carry warmth without committing you to anything. Save the rose for the point where you would be comfortable saying the sentence out loud.

faqs.question: How many flower emojis should I put in one message?
faqs.answer: One. A second flower does not double the signal — it shifts the register from sincere to decorative, and a row of three or more reads as visual punctuation rather than as meaning. If one character is not carrying enough, the fix is a sentence, not a longer string of glyphs.

faqs.question: Does the tulip emoji mean something different from the rose?
faqs.answer: Yes. 🌷 (Unicode character name TULIP, U+1F337) reads as affection with no pressure attached, while 🌹 (ROSE, U+1F339) reads as a romantic declaration. The tulip is what people reach for when they like someone and are not yet defining the relationship.

faqs.question: How do I reply if my girlfriend sends me a rose?
faqs.answer: Match the register, not the glyph. A bouquet after good news wants a thank-you in words; a rose from a partner wants a sentence back rather than another rose, because a mirrored emoji reads as acknowledgement without content. Repeating the same character is the most common way a reply lands flat.

faqs.question: Does a flower emoji mean the same thing to my parents as it does to my friends?
faqs.answer: No, and there is survey evidence for the gap. Zhukova and Herring's 2024 study in Language@Internet found younger respondents rated the smile and thumbs-up emojis as more passive-aggressive, while older respondents rated the fire and bomb emojis more negatively. Assume the older reader takes the flower literally and the younger one may not.

faqs.question: Is the bouquet emoji only for congratulations?
faqs.answer: Mostly. 💐 (BOUQUET, U+1F490) marks an occasion — a result, a promotion, a thank-you — which is why it is the safest flower emoji to send someone you are not close to. It is a poor fit inside an apology, where the celebratory reading fights the message.

faqs.question: Can I use a flower emoji in an apology?
faqs.answer: Only alongside the apology, never instead of it. Rodrigues and colleagues found that for more serious negative replies, emotional text signalled greater relationship interest while emoji signalled less interest by making the message read as more negative. Write the explanation first; the flower can sit at the end of it.

faqs.question: Is there a flower emoji that reads as friendship rather than romance?
faqs.answer: 🌻 (SUNFLOWER, U+1F33B) and 💐 are the two that stay clear of romance. Sunflower reads as encouragement aimed at someone — exam results, a hard week — and bouquet reads as marking an occasion. Both are safe for a friend, a sibling or a colleague.

faqs.question: Do flower emojis count as flirting?
faqs.answer: 🌹 does, unambiguously. 🌷 and 🌸 are genuinely ambiguous and are read as flirting mainly when the surrounding message already leans that way. Because the reader decides, the safest assumption is that a flower emoji amplifies whatever your sentence already said rather than adding a new meaning of its own.

faqs.question: For a birthday, should I send the bouquet or the rose?
faqs.answer: 💐 for anyone, 🌹 only for a partner. The bouquet is the occasion-marking character, which is exactly what a birthday is, and it carries no romantic load. On SubhSandesh the birthday page for a partner is the #5 page type at 258 created and 7.6% of all pages, so the romantic version is a real but much smaller share of birthday messages.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Flower Emoji Meaning in Chat: What You Are Actually Sending

Flower emoji meaning in chat is set by the reader, not by the flower. 🌹 (Unicode character name ROSE) reads as romantic interest stated out loud; 🥀 (WILTED FLOWER, the glyph most people search for as the "dead flower emoji") reads as damage; 💐 (BOUQUET) reads as an occasion being marked rather than a feeling being confessed.

That reading almost always happens on a phone. On SubhSandesh, 50.2% of shared pages are opened on a phone (20,937 of 41,682 views), and it is the phone that supplies the picture — so the artwork you tapped is not reliably the artwork they see. The digital bouquet is our #2 page type, at 796 created and 23.4% of all pages.

What follows is what each of the six most-sent flower emojis does between two people, their verified Unicode names, and the case where an emoji is the wrong move and words are needed.

## What a flower emoji is in a chat window

A flower emoji is a single Unicode character that your device draws as a picture. The standard hands out a number and a name and stops there: 🌹 is code point U+1F339, character name ROSE. Nothing in that record specifies what the rose should look like.

The picture comes from a font the operating system ships. On a Mac that file is literally called Apple Color Emoji; Android, Windows and WhatsApp each supply their own. Two people in the same conversation are therefore looking at two different drawings of the same character.

That is the gap the emoji dictionaries leave open. They give a character's name and code point accurately; what they do not give is what happens between two people when one of them sends it — the question behind almost every search for flower emoji meaning in chat, on WhatsApp or in a DM.

## Six flower emojis people actually send, and what each one signals

Twelve characters in the Unicode Character Database, version 16.0.0, carry a flower as their character name. Six do nearly all the work in real conversations. Each entry gives the code point, the character name, what it tends to read as, and when to avoid it.

### 1. 💐 U+1F490 BOUQUET — "this is an occasion"

The bouquet marks an event: a result, a promotion, a new job, a thank-you. It is the least romantically loaded of the flower emojis, which makes it the safe one to send a colleague or a cousin.

Sent to a partner with no occasion attached, it reads faintly formal — closer to a card than a confession. Avoid it inside an apology, where celebration imagery fights the message.

### 2. 🌹 U+1F339 ROSE — "I mean this romantically"

The rose is the only flower emoji almost everyone reads as an explicit romantic statement. That is its strength and its risk: it removes ambiguity, so it also removes deniability, which is exactly why people hesitate over it early on.

It also adds less than senders assume. In two experiments with a combined 451 participants, [Rodrigues and colleagues found that positive replies signalled the greatest relationship interest regardless of cue](https://repositorio.iscte-iul.pt/handle/10071/17081) — with emoji, with emotional text, or with neither. A rose after a warm message is decoration; a rose instead of one is a substitution.

### 3. 🥀 U+1F940 WILTED FLOWER — "something is wrong between us"

Unicode's name for this character is WILTED FLOWER, even though the query people type is "dead flower emoji". It is one of the very few flower emojis with genuine negative force, and sending it on purpose is a deliberate act.

Read it as damage rather than sadness: a wilted rose points at a thing that used to be alive. Avoid sending it to someone who cannot ask you what you meant.

### 4. 🌷 U+1F337 TULIP — "affection, with no pressure"

The tulip is the rose's low-stakes cousin: warmth without the declaration, which makes it the workhorse for someone you like and are not yet defining.

It is also the most commonly misread of the six, because much of its audience treats it as purely decorative. If the affection is the point, put it in words and let the tulip agree with them.

### 5. 🌸 U+1F338 CHERRY BLOSSOM — softening, not stating

Cherry blossom rarely carries content. It softens the sentence it is attached to, much as a smile at the end of one does, and it works as visual punctuation more than as meaning.

Because it softens, it can also blunt. A cherry blossom on a serious message makes that message read as less serious than you intended.

### 6. 🌻 U+1F33B SUNFLOWER — "cheer up"

Sunflower is the encouragement flower: exam results, a bad week, a hospital visit. It reads as brightness aimed at someone, which is not the same as affection aimed at someone.

That distinction matters when the recipient is not looking for cheer. Aimed at grief it reads as dismissal — the most common way a well-meant flower emoji lands badly.

## Which flower emoji maps to which kind of message

The table pairs each character with its verified code point and the SubhSandesh page type that carries the same message at length, measured 2026-09-02 across 3,397 pages created since 2026-03-12.

| Emoji | Unicode character name | Code point | Nearest SubhSandesh page type (created, share of 3,397) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 💐 | BOUQUET | U+1F490 | digital bouquet — 796 created, 23.4% |
| 🌹 | ROSE | U+1F339 | "I love you" page — 996 created, 29.3% |
| 🥀 | WILTED FLOWER | U+1F940 | apology dashboard — 740 created, 21.8% |
| 🌷 | TULIP | U+1F337 | Darling romantic page — 349 created, 10.3% |
| 🌻 | SUNFLOWER | U+1F33B | birthday page for a partner — 258 created, 7.6% |

The right-hand column is the useful part: the messages people build a whole page around are the same five the flower emojis compress into a character. If a rose is carrying more than one character can hold, a [hand-tied digital bouquet you send as a link](https://subhsandesh.in/bouquet-gf) or an ["I love you" page built around your own photos](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) is the long form of the same sentence.

## The dead flower emoji: what 🥀 is doing when someone sends it

The force of U+1F940 comes from being the only wilted thing in a set of healthy ones. Set against 💐 and 🌹, 🥀 is a marked choice, and marked choices carry weight.

In practice it does three jobs: it signals a relationship in trouble, it signals grief or loss, or — increasingly — it signals aesthetic melancholy with no referent at all, the way a sad-song lyric in a bio does.

Which of the three you are receiving depends almost entirely on who sent it. That ambiguity is not a flaw in your reading; it is what a one-glyph message does. When 🥀 arrives from a partner mid-argument, an [interactive apology page that says what actually went wrong](https://subhsandesh.in/apology-dashboard) is the reply that resolves it, and a matching emoji is the reply that does not.

## Why the same flower emoji lands differently on WhatsApp, Instagram and iPhone

Three separate things are going on, and it is worth keeping them apart. The first is rendering: because each vendor draws its own artwork, your rose and their rose are different pictures, and tone travels with pictures.

The second is platform convention. [Tim Highfield's 2018 study of emoji and hashtags in *First Monday*](https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/view/9398) compared user-led emoji hashtags on Instagram against platform-directed hashtag emoji on Twitter, showing how platforms variously support and restrict their users' platform vernaculars. A flower in an Instagram comment is often audience-facing decoration; the same flower in a WhatsApp thread is addressed to one person.

The third is the reader. [Zhukova and Herring's 2024 survey in *Language@Internet*](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/li/article/view/40800) found younger respondents rated the smile and thumbs-up emojis as more passive-aggressive, while older respondents rated the fire and bomb emojis more negatively — same characters, different verdicts by generation. A study of emoji miscommunication among Nigerian youths lands in the same place from another direction, concluding that [users need to recognise the potential for misinterpretation and that emoji literacy matters](https://journals.mmupress.com/index.php/jiwe/article/view/848).

## When a flower emoji is the wrong move

Here is the case against everything above, including against us. For serious messages the emoji is the wrong instrument and words are the right one.

The Rodrigues study is unusually direct about this. For more serious negative replies, emotional text signalled greater relationship interest by increasing the message's positivity, while emoji signalled *less* interest by increasing its negativity. A 🥀 sent instead of an explanation makes things measurably worse.

There is a structural reason. In a formal semantic account of emoji-text combinations, [Grosz, Kaiser and Pierini argue that face emoji are expressive elements anchored to an attitude holder that comment on a proposition provided by the accompanying text](https://www.glossa-journal.org/article/id/9128/) — their case studies cover face and activity emoji, not flowers, but the shape of the claim holds. An emoji comments on a sentence; remove the sentence and there is nothing left to comment on.

SubhSandesh loses in the same place. Our pages take work — the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 6.9 hours, sampled on the "I love you" page across 996 pages — so if this has to land in the next ninety seconds, type the sentence. And 50.2% of views being on a phone cuts both ways: a recipient without a smartphone is better served by a phone call than by any link we can generate.

## Sources

- Zhukova, M. & Herring, S. C. (2024). [Benign or Toxic? Differences in Emoji Interpretation by Gender, Generation, and Emoji Type](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/li/article/view/40800). *Language@Internet* 22, 74–108. Published 20 December 2024.
- Rodrigues, D., Lopes, D., Prada, M., Thompson, D. & Garrido, M. V. (2017). [A frown emoji can be worth a thousand words: perceptions of emoji use in text messages exchanged between romantic partners](https://repositorio.iscte-iul.pt/handle/10071/17081). *Telematics and Informatics*. Published 2017.
- Grosz, P., Kaiser, E. & Pierini, F. (2023). [Discourse anaphoricity vs. perspective sensitivity in emoji semantics](https://www.glossa-journal.org/article/id/9128/). *Glossa: a journal of general linguistics* 8(1). Published July 2023.
- Highfield, T. (2018). [Emoji hashtags // hashtag emoji: Of platforms, visual affect, and discursive flexibility](https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/view/9398). *First Monday* 23(9). Published 1 September 2018.
- Udoudom, U., William, G., Igiri, A., Okon, E. & Aruku, K. (2024). [Emojis and Miscommunication in Text-Based Interactions Among Nigerian Youths](https://journals.mmupress.com/index.php/jiwe/article/view/848). *Journal of Informatics and Web Engineering* 3(1), 226–240. Published 14 February 2024.

Code points and character names were checked directly against the Unicode Character Database, version 16.0.0. No claim about which Unicode release first carried a character appears above, because we could not verify one.

failed.item: Slug short, hyphenated, lowercase, no stop words
failed.why: flower-emoji-meaning-in-chat contains the stop word "in". Counted deliberately rather than assumed: the slug is 5 segments, lowercase and hyphenated, but "in" is a stop word and cannot be dropped without breaking exact-match against the target keyword "flower emoji meaning in chat", which is itself 5 words. Removing it would give flower-emoji-meaning-chat, which no longer matches the query and was not the slug verified free against the 935 live articles.

auditReport.honestAssessment: This SERP is owned by the emoji reference works and they are correct about the glyphs, so the post does not try to out-dictionary them: it is the only page on the query that treats a flower emoji as a relational act and cites emoji-interpretation research (Zhukova & Herring 2024) and romantic-messaging experiments (Rodrigues et al. 2017, N = 451) to argue that the receiver, not the glyph, fixes the meaning — plus a glyph-to-page-type mapping across 3,397 real pages that nobody else can print. An answer engine asked "what does 🥀 mean when he sends it" has nothing else on this SERP to lift. What it cannot overcome: emojipedia.org and the purpose-built emoji dictionaries hold the topical authority and the backlinks for the head term, so a rank win on "flower emoji meaning" is not a realistic expectation and no outcome is being predicted here. Two honest gaps: the pricing block in facts.md is empty, so the post makes no cost claim in any direction, and the strongest available cross-platform-rendering paper (Miller et al. 2016 on emoji interpretation across platforms) is already spent in USED-SOURCES.md, so the vendor-artwork claim rests on a directly verified local check (Apple Color Emoji ships on macOS; the Unicode Character Database 16.0.0 records a code point and a character name and no artwork) rather than on a citation.
